prize: Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2026, Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford, "for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation" (nobelprize.org press release, 12 October 2026)

committee.source: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, popular information on the 2026 prize in economic sciences
committee.hall: Hall's hypothesis was that changes in consumption could not be predicted because they depend on new – and thus unpredictable – information.
committee.hall_mishkin: They used microdata for a number of individual households, showing that around 80 per cent of them made their consumption decisions in line with the theory, while the rest lived hand-to-mouth.
committee.sb_source: Scientific background on the 2026 prize in economic sciences, PDF p. 25 (printed p. 23)
committee.sb_hall_mishkin: allow a fraction of consumption to move hand in hand with current income and estimate this hand-to-mouth fraction in the panel data to be 20% (whereas the other 80% follow the prediction of the rational-expectations, permanent-income hypothesis)
committee.sb_hall_mishkin_sample: food consumption, 2,309 US families (Panel Study of Income Dynamics), 1969-1975

method.checked_against: statsmodels 0.14.4 and SciPy 1.15.2, to 1e-8 (tests/statsmodels_reference.json); neither is a dependency
method.hac: Newey-West (Bartlett kernel), 4 lags, no small-sample factor; F tests use F(q, n - k)
method.iv: two-stage least squares; HAC covariance from the structural residuals; 95 % interval = lambda +/- 1.96 standard errors
method.effective_F: Montiel Olea and Pflueger (2013): pi' Z'Z pi / tr(V Z'Z), V = HAC covariance of the first-stage coefficients pi, constant partialled out
method.strong_rule: instruments are called strong only if the effective F (Montiel Olea and Pflueger 2013; HAC, Bartlett, 4 lags) is above 10; the classic first-stage F assumes homoskedastic, serially uncorrelated errors. Their own conservative 5 % test for a worst-case bias below 10 % needs an effective F above 23.11
method.anderson_rubin: Anderson-Rubin (1949) 95 % set: the values lambda0 at which the instruments do not predict dc - lambda0 * dy (HAC Wald F below its 5 % critical value), searched on a grid of step 0.001 from -10 to 20. It stays valid however weak the instruments are, but it tests lambda0 together with the model's other restrictions, so it can exclude the two-stage least squares estimate, or be empty when the model with a constant lambda is rejected at every value. Its HAC F test rejects too often in samples this size (see the control), so the HAC set is likely too narrow; the same set with the classic (homoskedastic) F is reported next to it

fisher.formula: relative_t = sqrt(L_t x P_t), L_t = sum_i v_i,t-1 r_i,t / sum_i v_i,t-1, P_t = sum_i v_i,t / sum_i (v_i,t / r_i,t), with r_i,t = q_i,t / q_i,t-1 (q: BEA's quantity index, v: BEA's current-dollar value); the level is the chained product of the relatives, scaled so that its 2017 average equals the 2017 average of current-dollar non-durables plus services (chained 2017 dollars)

fisher_check.what: Fisher chain of DDURRA, DNDGRA, DSERRA (weights DDURRC, DNDGRC, DSERRC) against BEA's DPCERA

choices.consumption: real spending on non-durable goods and services, Fisher-chained from BEA's quantity indexes DNDGRA and DSERRA with the current-dollar values DNDGRC and DSERRC (chained 2017 dollars)
choices.why_nds: Hall (1978) and Campbell and Mankiw (1989) used spending on non-durable goods and services, and so do we. BEA's quarterly file has chained-dollar non-durables (DNDGRX) and services (DSERRX) only from 2007Q1, and chained-dollar components do not add up to a total; but it has BEA's Fisher quantity indexes (DNDGRA, DSERRA) and current-dollar values (DNDGRC, DSERRC) from 1947Q1, which is all a Fisher chain needs. The same formula applied to durables, non-durables and services reproduces BEA's own total-PCE quantity index (DPCERA) (see fisher_check). Total real PCE (DPCERX), which includes durable goods, is kept as a robustness check; under Hall's hypothesis spending on durables need not be a random walk (Mankiw 1982)
choices.robustness: total real personal consumption expenditures (DPCERX), which includes durable goods
choices.why_population: B230RC is the population line of NIPA Table 2.1 (line 40), the one BEA itself uses for its per-capita income and spending series (Table 7.1, Selected Per Capita Product and Income Series)
choices.why_start: the regressions start in 1953Q1, the start of Campbell and Mankiw's sample (1953:1 to 1986:4); with four lags of quarterly growth they need data from 1951Q4. BEA's quarterly series, income included, start in 1947Q1
choices.chained_2017_check: chained dollars equal current dollars in the reference year: the 2017 average of DPCERX equals that of current-dollar PCE (DPCERC) in this vintage, 13,290,625.5 million
choices.per_capita: chained 2017 dollars per person (annual rate); growth = 100 x change in the log, in log points (about per cent)

out_of_sample.method: each quarter from 1990 on is predicted by the regression fitted on all earlier quarters; R^2 against the mean of all earlier quarters (negative = worse than that mean)
out_of_sample.benchmark_note: the benchmark is the average of all earlier quarters; average growth was lower after 1990 than before

hall.time_aggregation: Quarterly figures are averages over the quarter, so even if spending followed a random walk, its change from one quarter to the next would be correlated with the previous change (Working 1960), and the first lag would predict it under Hall's hypothesis; lags two to four are not affected (Campbell and Mankiw 1989, p. 190)

hall_1978.consumption: consumption of nondurables and services in 1972 dollars from the U.S. National Income and Product Accounts divided by the population
hall_1978.income_test: Table 3, equation 3.2: consumption per person on its first lag and four lags of real disposable income per person, in levels
hall_1978.income_test_quote: The F-statistic for the joint predictive value of all four lagged income variables is 2.0, somewhat less than the critical value of 2.4 at the 5 percent level.
hall_1978.ours: the growth-rate version: the change in log consumption per person on lags of its own growth and of income growth

hall.plain: Using spending and income growth from two to four quarters back, a regression explains 11.5 % of the quarter-to-quarter changes in US spending per person on non-durables and services, 1953Q1 to 2019Q4 (in-sample; 9.4 % adjusted for the number of lags), and 2.9 % for 1953Q1 to 2026Q2. With the most recent quarter added (lags 1-4) the shares are 22.0 % and 11.9 %, but part of that is the averaging within quarters.

published.time_aggregation: We deal with this problem by lagging the instruments more than one period, so there is at least a two-period time gap between the instruments and the variables in equation (1.4).
published.about_half: When we use instruments that are jointly significant for predicting income growth at the 5% level or better, we get estimates of λ, the fraction of the population that consumes its current income, of about 0.5.

a.question: From the last year of data, how much of next quarter's change in US consumer spending can be predicted? (0-100 %)
a.reads_as: predictors = spending and income growth per person two to four quarters back; share of the variance of next quarter's growth in spending on non-durables and services explained (R^2, in-sample)
a.why_lags_2_4: Quarterly figures are averages over the quarter, so even if spending followed a random walk, its change from one quarter to the next would be correlated with the previous change (Working 1960), and the first lag would predict it under Hall's hypothesis; lags two to four are not affected (Campbell and Mankiw 1989, p. 190)
a.why_to_2019: 2020-2021 are left out because in those quarters spending and income per person moved by many times their usual quarterly change, often in opposite directions (2020Q2: spending -10.2, income +9.4 log points; before 2020 the standard deviation of quarterly growth was 0.47 for spending and 0.86 for income), so a few quarters dominate the fit; with lags they also reach into the following quarters, so the sample stops at 2019Q4. The full sample is reported next to it.
